definition: Repress means to hold something down by force, or to push an unwanted feeling or memory out of your own mind.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word repress. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know repress should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The junta repressed even mourning, posting soldiers at the cemetery gates on each anniversary of the massacre.
Curb is far gentler than repress — the light rein, a rule that trims a habit's edges and leaves the habit alive, while repressing puts real weight on top and holds the thing down.
Crush goes further than repress — a repressed movement survives underground, waiting; a crushed one is gone.

Put down is the plain, finished phrase for breaking a rising by force — the revolt was put down, and the story ends there. Repress names the longer weight: a repressed strike or feeling is held down continuously and may still be pushing back underneath.

To stamp out is to keep applying force until nothing is left standing — the plot, the practice, the last ember, gone. To repress is to hold down something that still exists: a repressed movement survives under the weight, waiting for it to lift.

In 1848 the kingdom's reformers discovered that dinner was illegal.

Political meetings were banned, so the opposition held banquets instead — toasts as speeches, menus as manifestos — until the crown saw through the tablecloths and set about repressing the banquets too.
Gatherings of more than twenty now required a permit; permits were never granted; and the cavalry learned the address of every hall in the capital that could seat a hundred.
Repress is the exact word for the crown's answer, because to repress is to hold something down by force — the banquets did not end because appetites changed.
Restrain, this unit's gentler cousin, holds a thing back to keep it under control; repress puts the state's whole weight on top of it and sits.
Repress is the historian's verb for force from above: strikes, uprisings, and mourning get repressed, and so — in the mind's own police state — do memories and feelings.
Restrain is protective or neutral, a hold rather than a weight; impede merely slows; and the same crackdown done with licenses and ledgers instead of cavalry usually goes by suppression.

For forty years the governors repressed the island's carnival rather than abolish it on paper.
Each spring the square filled with soldiers, the organizers paid their fines, and the drums went into the customs house until summer.
And each spring the carnival survived anyway — rehearsed in kitchens, drummed on table edges, taught to children as a game.
The weight never lifted and the thing beneath it never died; the two simply pressed against each other for a generation.
When the governors finally sailed home, the carnival walked back into the square as if it had been waiting by the gate.
